questions.question: Explain the difference between economic growth and economic development, describe how the Human Development Index is constructed, and interpret the gap between South Africa's income ranking and its HDI ranking.
questions.expected_answer: Growth answers a counting question — real GDP rose; development answers a living question — lives became longer, healthier, better schooled, less poor. The HDI blends three dimensions into one score between 0 and 1: income (GNI per person adjusted for buying power), health (life expectancy at birth) and education (expected and actual years of schooling). South Africa ranks upper-middle on income but noticeably lower on the HDI: the gap is the development deficit itself — South Africans die younger and learn less than a country producing this much should allow, meaning growth has not been converted into development.

questions.question: List the six common characteristics of developing countries and demonstrate, using two of them, why South Africa is only a partial fit that must be explained rather than a clean fit.
questions.expected_answer: The six: low standard of living; low productivity; rapid population growth with heavy dependency burdens; large-scale unemployment and underemployment; dependence on the primary sector and raw exports; deficient infrastructure and incomplete markets. Partial fits: on living standards South Africa's average income is respectable but the distribution is among the most unequal ever measured, so millions live in absolute poverty inside a comfortable-looking average — the problem is the spread, not the average; on primary dependence, production is service-dominated yet export earnings still lean on platinum, gold, coal and iron ore, so commodity-price swings still run through the trade accounts. (Unemployment is the opposite case — not partial but extreme: above 30% official, above 40% expanded.)

questions.question: Argue the economic case for Indigenous Knowledge Systems as a development asset, and use the hoodia and rooibos cases to explain what biopiracy is and how the law should respond.
questions.expected_answer: IKS supplies working development infrastructure built on trust: stokvels rotate pooled monthly savings worth tens of billions of rands a year among people banks historically excluded, and burial societies extend the model into insurance; drought-hardy sorghum and millet, intercropping and communal work parties supply agricultural resilience; traditional healers, recognised in law, reach the majority of patients; customary institutions govern communal land. Development that ignores trusted institutions predictably fails, so policy should build on them. Biopiracy is profiting from indigenous knowledge without consent or compensation: San knowledge of hoodia was patented for appetite-suppressant products without permission or payment, and only years of dispute produced a benefit-sharing agreement; rooibos communities won recognition and now earn a negotiated share. The legal response: indigenous knowledge legislation, compulsory benefit-sharing and recording traditional knowledge so it cannot be patented as new.
